messages.subject: plotting predicted relationship with covariates
parts:
Hello Inla Group,

I ran an inlabru zap model with several covariates. Please find the summary of my model attached.
I plotted my predicted presence and count ( see picture 2 for the predicted count  attached) using the code below. But I want to plot the relationship between my count and each covariate ( e.g. dichla on my court).  Can anyone suggest how to plot these relationships?  

Thank you in advance
Morgane

pred_zap_dichla <- predict(
  fit_zap_dichla,
  gannet_fvcom_nohigh_sf,
  ~ {
    presence_prob <-
    plogis(horiz_speed_std  + Intercept_present)
    lambda <- exp(bottom_temp_std+dichla_std+ field + Intercept_count)
    expect <- presence_prob * lambda * area / (1 - exp(-lambda * area))
    variance <- expect * (1 - exp(-lambda * area) * expect)
    list(
      presence = presence_prob,
      lambda = lambda,
      expect = expect,
      variance = variance,
      obs_prob = (1 - presence_prob) * (count == 0) +
        (count > 0) * presence_prob * dpois(count, expect) / (1 - dpois(0, expect))
    )
  },
  n.samples = 1000
)
presence_zap_dichla <- pred_zap_dichla$presence
expect_zap_dichla <- pred_zap_dichla$expect
expect_zap_dichla$pred_var <- pred_zap_dichla$variance$mean + expect_zap_dichla$sd^2
expect_zap_dichla$log_score <- -log(pred_zap_dichla$obs_prob$mean)

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] plotting predicted relationship with covariates
parts:
Hi Morgane,
fundamentally, the spatial location information is just a special type
of covariate, and your 2nd figure illustrates how the predicted count
varies with that covariate. So if you're happy with just plotting the
information for the encountered covariate values, you could just make
a plot with the covariate of interest on the x-axis. However, just as
for the spatial plot, that gives you the "aggregate" behaviour, when
all variables change according to what combinations were observed. If
what you're looking for is "the dependence on a covariate, keeping all
other covariates fixed", you'll need to construct a data frame with
such "data", for use in the prediction; let it have the same structure
as your original data, but vary only the covariate of interest,
keeping all other covariates to some fixed value at which you want to
observe the effect of the special covariate. Note that since the
predictor depends on all those values, the resulting figure will be
different depending on what values you set the other variables to.
This is a basic issue in multi-input models that there's no real way
around, except for specific types of models where the structural
assumptions allow simplifications (e.g. with log-odds ratios in
logistic regression).
Finn
